etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English here, hir, hire, from Old English hire (“her”), from Proto-Germanic *hezōi (dative and genitive singular of *hijō).

Cognate with North Frisian hör, Saterland Frisian hier, hiere (“her”), West Frisian har (“her”), Dutch haar (“her”), German Low German hör (“her”), German ihr (“her”).

definitions.definition: Belonging to her (belonging to that female person or animal, or in poetic or old-fashioned language that ship, city, season, etc).

quote.citation: 1928, The Journal of the American Dental Association, page 765:
quote.text: Prodigal in everything, summer spreads her blessings with lavish unconcern, and waving her magic wand across the landscape of the world, she bids the sons of men to enter in [...]

quote.citation: 1932, Delos W. Lovelace, King Kong, published 1965, page 1:
quote.text: Her crew knew that deep in her heart beat engines fit and able to push her blunt old nose ahead at a sweet fourteen knots, come Hell or high water.

quote.citation: 2001, Betsy Gould Hearne, Wishes, Kisses, and Pigs, Simon and Schuster, →ISBN, page 78:
quote.text: On top of the circle she wrote her name, Louise, just above where the 12 on a clock would be.

quote.citation: 2010, Andrew Lambert, Nelson: Britannia's God of War, Faber & Faber, →ISBN:
quote.text: On 24 April Nelson rejoined his ship, her battle damage repaired  […]

definitions.definition: Belonging to a person of unspecified gender (to counterbalance the traditional "his" in this sense).

quote.citation: 2017, David Yellin, Essentials of Integrating the Language Arts, page 115:
quote.text: Begin by having students choose a short poem to memorize; they will enjoy searching the library for a poem that appeals to them. If a student wishes to memorize her poem and share it aloud with the rest of the class, suggest a buddy system.

definitions.definition: The form of she used after a preposition, as the object of a verb, or (colloquial) as a subject with a conjunction; that woman, that ship, etc, or (dialect) as a subject without a conjunction.

quote.citation: February 1896, Ground-swells, by Jeannette H. Walworth, published in Lippincott's Monthly Magazine; page 183:
quote.text:
"Then what became of her?"
"Her? Which ‘her’? The park is full of ‘hers’."
"The lady with the green feathers in her hat. A big Gainsborough hat. I am quite sure it was Miss Hartuff."

quote.citation: 1913, D. H. Lawrence, Sons and Lovers, Penguin Lawrence Edition, Penguin, published 1994, →ISBN, page 213:
quote.text: “I’ll bet ’er wor a toe-rag,” said Morel, following up his joke. ¶ “Don’t you be so cheeky about a queen,” said Annie.

quote.citation: 1950, C. S. Lewis, The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe:
quote.text: "It's all right," he was shouting. "Come out, Mrs. Beaver. Come out, Sons and Daughters of Adam and Eve. It's all right! It isn't her!" This was bad grammar of course, but that is how beavers talk when they are excited; I mean, in Narnia—in our world they usually don't talk at all.

quote.citation: 2013, James Tully, The Crimes of Charlotte Brontë:
quote.text: Every day I had to watch as him and her went off for long walks together, and each night I had to go to my lonely, cold bed with the thought that they were sharing the same one  […]
[…]  daring dizzying passages in other, fleeting and passionate dwellings within the hims and hers whom she inhabits  […]

quote.citation: 2004, Charles J. Sullivan, Love and Survival, page 68:
quote.text: By this time, she had so many questions, but she only hit him up for one answer about those “hims” and “hers.” She asked, “Do both hims and hers reproduce hummers?”
